$17 an Hour Is How Much a Year? $35,360 Full-Time, Before Taxes

Direct Answer$17 an hour is $35,360 a year full-time ($680 a week, $2,946.67 a month) before taxes. Schedules, overtime, unpaid weeks, and federal take-home inside.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 30, 2026•Updated November 3, 2026•9 min read•Hourly Wage Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: $35,360 a Year$17 an Hour in Every Pay Period$17 an Hour at Different SchedulesWhat Overtime AddsWhat Unpaid Weeks Cost$17 an Hour After Taxes (Federal Only)$17 vs Nearby RatesIs $17 an Hour a Good Wage?How to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

Full-time, $17 an hour comes to $35,360 a year before taxes. That's $680 a week and $2,946.67 a month.

The Short Answer: $35,360 a Year

Work a standard full-time schedule — 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year — and $17 an hour adds up to $35,360 a year before taxes. The math is just one multiplication: hourly rate × hours per week × weeks per year. Here that's $17 × 40 × 52 = $35,360, or 2,080 paid hours across the year. The rest of this guide is really just variations on that one number: fewer hours, overtime, unpaid weeks, and what taxes take out of it.

If you're weighing an hourly offer against a salary, $35,360 is the number to line up next to it — before taxes, benefits, or time off on either side get in the way. It also clears up the question behind the question: a $35,000 salary and $17 an hour are pretty much the same deal, since $35,000 a year works out to $16.83 an hour.

$17 an Hour in Every Pay Period

Same rate, six different views. Every number below is gross pay, before taxes or deductions:

PeriodHoursGross Pay
Hour1$17.00
Day (8 hours)8$136.00
Week (40 hours)40$680.00
Biweekly (80 hours)80$1,360.00
Semi-monthly (24 checks)—$1,473.33
Month (average)173.33$2,946.67
Year (2,080 hours)2,080$35,360.00

Figure 1: $17 an hour across pay periods. The semi-monthly check is larger only because there are fewer of them — the year is the same.

One thing to watch with the monthly line: $2,946.67 is an average. A four-week month pays $2,720, and a three-paycheck biweekly month pays $4,080 gross. Pay periods just don't line up neatly with calendar months, which is why some months feel leaner than others. Use the average for your budget. Our biweekly vs semi-monthly guide and our three-paycheck months guide walk through both quirks in full.

$17 an Hour at Different Schedules

Not everyone works 40 hours. Run the same rate at different weekly hours and the year looks very different:

Hours per weekWeeklyMonthly (average)Annual
20 (part-time)$340.00$1,473.33$17,680.00
25 (part-time)$425.00$1,841.67$22,100.00
30 (part-time)$510.00$2,210.00$26,520.00
35$595.00$2,578.33$30,940.00
40 (full-time)$680.00$2,946.67$35,360.00

Two schedule details catch people off guard. First, a 37.5-hour paid week — pretty common when your daily lunch break is unpaid and doesn't count toward paid hours — comes to $33,150 a year. That's $2,210 less than the full 40-hour figure, even though the job still takes up your whole week. Second, part-time roles often skip the benefits a full-time role comes with, so look at the whole package, not just the hourly number. Our full-time hours guide explains where the 40-hour line comes from.

What Overtime Adds

Overtime is where hourly pay pulls ahead of a salary. At time-and-a-half, every overtime hour pays $25.50 instead of $17. Say you pick up 5 overtime hours every week, all year long:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay40 hours × $17$680.00 per week
Step 2 — Overtime rate$17 × 1.5$25.50 per hour
Step 3 — Overtime pay5 hours × $25.50$127.50 per week
Step 4 — Weekly total$680 + $127.50$807.50 per week
Annual total$807.50 × 52$41,990.00

That's $6,630 of overtime pay on top of the $35,360 base — nearly a 19% bump for five extra hours a week. It comes with three conditions, though: you need to be non-exempt (overtime-eligible), you actually have to work those hours, and your employer has to pay overtime past 40 hours in a week. Salaried exempt workers don't get any of this. Our overtime tax guide clears up the myth that overtime gets taxed at a higher rate.

What Unpaid Weeks Cost

That $35,360 assumes every one of the 52 weeks is paid. Every unpaid week costs you exactly one week's pay — $680 at this rate:

Paid weeksUnpaid weeksAnnual gross
52 (full year)0$35,360.00
502$34,000.00
484$32,640.00

Paid vacation and holidays don't shrink the total — you're paid for those weeks. Only unpaid time off cuts into the year. So when an offer quotes $17 an hour, ask how many weeks are actually paid. The gap between 52 and 48 paid weeks is $2,720, which is a full month of average gross pay at this rate.

$17 an Hour After Taxes (Federal Only)

Gross pay isn't what you get to spend. For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, here's our federal-only estimate. State tax, 401(k), and health premiums aren't in it, so your real paycheck will be smaller:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay$17 × 2,080 hours$35,360.00
Step 2 — Standard deductionSingle filer, 2026− $16,100.00
Step 3 — Taxable income$35,360 − $16,100$19,260.00
Step 4 — Federal income tax10% × $12,400 + 12% × $6,860$2,063.20
Step 5 — FICA$35,360 × 7.65% (SS $2,192.32 + Medicare $512.72)$2,705.04
Take-home (federal only)$35,360 − $2,063.20 − $2,705.04$30,591.76

That works out to $2,549.31 a month on average, or $1,176.61 per biweekly paycheck, before state tax. Two rates are worth keeping apart: your marginal bracket is 12% (the rate on your last dollars), but your effective federal rate is only 5.8% ($2,063.20 ÷ $35,360), because the first $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10%. After federal taxes alone, you keep 86.5% of gross. The FICA piece uses the same 7.65% we break down in our FICA guide, and the same annual-liability method is behind our paycheck tax guide. That's also why some online calculators give you a slightly different number: they annualize one paycheck's withholding instead of working out the year's liability. Our pay stub guide shows where each of these lines shows up on a real stub.

Honesty note: this estimate treats all $35,360 as wages for both income tax and FICA, with no pre-tax deductions. Put money into a 401(k) and the income-tax lines drop, though the FICA lines stay put; health premiums through a cafeteria plan lower both.

$17 vs Nearby Rates

Small hourly differences add up fast — $3 an hour is $6,240 a year. Here's $17 next to its neighbors, plus two salaries readers often compare it with:

Pay levelHourly equivalentAnnual grossDifference from $17/hr
$15 an hour$15.00$31,200.00− $4,160
$17 an hour$17.00$35,360.00—
$20 an hour$20.00$41,600.00+ $6,240
$30 an hour$30.00$62,400.00+ $27,040
$30,000 salary$14.42$30,000.00− $5,360
$40,000 salary$19.23$40,000.00+ $4,640

The one that surprises people: $17 an hour full-time beats a $30,000 salary by $5,360 gross — and overtime only widens that gap. Flip it around and a $40,000 salary beats $17 an hour by $4,640, and you'd need steady overtime to close that, not the odd extra shift. When you're comparing offers, start with annual gross, then take-home, then benefits and paid weeks. Our $15 guide, $20 guide, and $30 guide all use the same method, so the four line up directly.

Is $17 an Hour a Good Wage?

Measured against the country as a whole, $17 an hour is a decent entry-level rate — with real limits. It's more than double the $7.25 federal minimum wage, and it's what you'll see for retail, warehouse, food-service, and entry-level support jobs, where the rate reflects the work rather than a license or a degree. But the median hourly wage in the United States is around $22–23 an hour in recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data, so $17 sits roughly a quarter below the middle of the market.

But "good" depends on where you live. In a low-cost city, $30,591.76 of federal-only take-home covers a modest life, especially with paid leave and employer health coverage. In a high-rent metro, that same money is tight on its own, and the extras matter more than the rate: paid weeks, health premiums, a retirement match, and reliable overtime hours. We'd judge the rate three ways: against the median, against your city's rent, and against the total package. A $17 rate with paid leave and a match is worth several thousand more than the same rate without them.

Limitations

A few things to keep in mind before you treat any figure above as your budget:

  1. State income tax isn't in here: most states tax income too, so real take-home is lower. The after-tax estimate is federal only.
  2. Benefits aren't counted: 401(k) contributions, health premiums, and other deductions come out of your check before you see it.
  3. Overtime isn't guaranteed: the $41,990 figure needs non-exempt status, actual overtime hours, and an employer that pays past 40 hours.
  4. The schedule matters: every figure uses the schedule stated in its section, and fewer hours or unpaid weeks change them all.
  5. Withholding vs. what you actually owe: one paycheck's withholding can differ from this annual estimate, and the difference settles when you file your return.
  6. This isn't tax advice: the take-home estimate uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. Credits, other income, and your filing status will change your real return.

Frequently Asked Questions

Here's what people ask us most about $17 an hour:

How much is $17 an hour a year?

It's $35,360 a year before taxes if you work full-time — $17 × 40 hours a week × 52 weeks. That breaks down to $2,946.67 a month on average, $1,360 in each biweekly paycheck, and $680 a week. Part-time hours, overtime, or unpaid weeks will shift that total. The schedules section above walks through each case.

How much is $17 an hour a month?

On average, $2,946.67 a month. That's just the annual $35,360 split by 12, though, so real months don't always match it. A four-week month brings in $2,720, and a three-paycheck biweekly month brings in $4,080 gross. Build your budget around the $2,946.67 average rather than any one month.

How much is $17 an hour biweekly?

Your biweekly paycheck would be $1,360 gross — 80 hours × $17 — paid 26 times a year. If your employer pays semi-monthly instead (24 paychecks), you'd get $1,473.33 per check. Either way the yearly total is the same; it's only how the pay is split up that changes. Mixing those two schedules up is one of the most common pay-period mistakes we see.

How much is $17 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer in 2026, our federal-only estimate comes to $30,591.76 a year. Start with $35,360 gross, take off $2,063.20 in federal income tax and $2,705.04 in FICA, and that's what's left. State income tax, 401(k) contributions, and health premiums would shrink the check further, and none of them are in this estimate.

Is $17 an hour a good wage?

Honestly, it depends on where you live and what comes with the job. At more than double the $7.25 federal minimum wage, $17 an hour is a decent entry-level rate, but it's still roughly a quarter below the national median hourly wage of around $22–23 an hour. Somewhere with low rent, paid leave, and benefits, it can stretch. In a high-rent city on its own, it's tight.

What is $17 an hour with overtime?

Say you pick up 5 overtime hours every week at time-and-a-half — that's $25.50 an hour — and you end the year at $41,990: $35,360 of regular pay plus $6,630 of overtime pay. That only holds if you're non-exempt, you actually work those hours, and your employer pays overtime past 40 hours a week.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $17 an hour is $35,360 a year full-time — $680 a week, $1,360 biweekly, $2,946.67 a month on average — before taxes.
  • Budget from the average month, not from any single month. Four-week months pay $2,720; three-paycheck months pay $4,080.
  • Five overtime hours a week add $6,630 a year ($41,990 total), if you're non-exempt and actually work them.
  • Each unpaid week costs $680. Ask how many weeks are paid before you accept any hourly offer.
  • Federal-only take-home is $30,591.76 for a single filer. Your marginal bracket is 12%, but your effective federal rate is just 5.8%.
  • Compare on annual gross first, then take-home, then benefits. $17 an hour beats a $30,000 salary by $5,360 gross.

Sources & Method

Here's how we got the numbers. Gross figures are based on a standard full-time year of 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks). Monthly averages are the annual total divided by 12, and biweekly figures assume 26 paychecks. The after-tax estimate uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: a $16,100 standard deduction, and brackets of 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, and 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32. FICA is 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), and the full $35,360 sits below that wage base. The median-wage comparison comes from recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data (roughly $22–23 an hour). State income tax, retirement contributions, health premiums, bonuses, and tips are left out unless a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Full-time, gross pay is $35,360 a year: $680 a week, $2,946.67 a month.
  2. Part-time hours, overtime, and unpaid weeks all change the total, and this guide works through each case.
  3. Whether $17 an hour covers a comfortable life comes down to your rent and where you live. In a high-rent metro, that same money is tight.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.

  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
